meta.program: The Four Moves · Manager Monday · Anchor's Edge · Vanderbilt
meta.audience: Vanderbilt people managers and team leads in the Anchor's Edge weekly rhythm. Works for 6 to 40 on a call; breakouts run in pairs. Assumes the April AI-exposure sessions; June closes the series year with From Insight to Action.
meta.roomSetup: Virtual, instructor led: camera on, deck link in chat, breakouts of 2 available. Learners follow on their own screens via the welcome-slide link or QR. Nothing typed into the deck is saved or sent.
meta.postSession: Seven days out, send the pulse: 'Did step one of your move happen? Which move did you call, and would you still call it? What does the owner need from you next?' Count of moves with a named owner and date is the Level 3 metric for the month.

full.description: The full 45-minute virtual session: every interaction runs live, breakouts run in pairs, and the capstone gets read-alouds. The per-section minutes on each slide sum to 45 including transitions.

core.description: The 30-minute slot: agenda and core-idea slides pass in stride, breakouts become solo passes with chat share-outs, debriefs shrink to one voice. Never cut the section interactions or the capstone.

meta.framework: ATD facilitator-guide structure: per module SAY / DO / ASK (with anticipated responses) / DEBRIEF / TRANSITION, plus preparation checklists, materials, contingencies, and a tough-questions bank.
materials: Meeting platform with screen share and breakout rooms; deck link ready to paste in chat
Facilitator machine with the facilitator edition open; notifications off
Learners on their own devices with the learner link
Chat open for share-outs; the capstone copy button pastes there cleanly

weekBefore: Run the learner edition start to finish and do every interaction honestly; you will demo at least one live.
Read this month's theme page on the Anchor's Edge dashboard so the goal tie-in is fluent.
Send the invite with the learner link and one line on what to bring.
dayBefore: Test screen share with the facilitator edition; confirm the notes rail is readable.
Open the learner link on a second device; the QR must land there.
Run the section interactions once so you can drive them without reading.
thirtyMinBefore: Welcome slide up as people join; link pasted in chat.
Close every other tab; silence the machine.

contingencies.if: Screen share or the site fails mid-session
contingencies.then: Paste the learner link in chat and narrate from your own browser; every interaction runs on learner devices without the share.
Run the breakout prompts as 60-second chat storms: everyone types their answer at once, you read the best three aloud.

contingencies.if: A manager says every insight on their map points to hire
contingencies.then: Run the order out loud: what would reskill look like here, what would redeploy look like, what would redesign look like? Hire earns its place only after those three answers exist.

contingencies.if: Someone names a real person while matching an insight to a move
contingencies.then: Protect them warmly and immediately: 'Hold that. Roles, never names.' The moves work on work, and the traffic light is firm: private information about people is red, never.

toughQuestions.q: Doesn't redesign just mean cutting jobs?
toughQuestions.a: Redesign here means rebuilding a role around the work that stays human: judgment, exceptions, relationships. Done early and openly, it protects people from the quiet version, where the role hollows out and the person gets blamed for it. Position changes are a separate process with HR; this session is how you avoid needing one.

toughQuestions.q: Can I use AI tools to analyze my team's data and pick the move?
toughQuestions.a: Run it through the traffic light. Generic scenarios and public research: green, go. Internal workload data: yellow, approved VU tools only. Anything private about individual people, their performance, health, or circumstances: red, never. The move decision itself stays human; it is a judgment call about people you know.

toughQuestions.q: What if my move needs budget or a requisition I don't control?
toughQuestions.a: Then step one is the ask, owned and dated like any other step. A specific sentence with a role, a reason, and a date is exactly what gets funded; vague reskilling themes are what get deferred. Bring it to the action-planning lab and your HR consultant with the sentence already written.

templates.title: Pre-work invite (paste into the calendar invite)
templates.body: Subject: Monday, 45 minutes on turning your AI map into a move. Dust off the AI-exposure map you built this spring, or just bring one honest observation about how AI has changed work on your team this year. Roles only, never names. Live and interactive; have the session link open on your own screen.

templates.title: 7-day pulse (send one week after)
templates.body: Subject: Did the move start? Three lines, reply whenever: 1) Did step one of the move on your card happen? 2) Which move did you call, and would you still call it? 3) What does the owner of the next step need from you?

sections.title: Welcome / QR
sections.purpose: Get everyone into the deck on their own screen and set the tone: 45 minutes, live, hands on.
sections.say: Welcome to Manager Monday. Scan the code or click the link in chat so this session runs on your screen too. Forty-five minutes, one focus: Translating AI insights into workforce moves.
facilitate: Slide up as people join; link pasted in chat every few minutes.
State the norm once: type into your own screen, nothing you enter is saved or sent.
sections.watchFor: People lurking without the deck open. The interactions only land if the deck is on their screen.
sections.transition: Before the topic, thirty seconds on why Vanderbilt is asking for this hour.

sections.title: Why we're here
sections.purpose: Anchor the session in the Chancellor's charge and name the goal this month serves, inside one minute.
sections.say: One sentence from the Chancellor sits over everything we do: Vanderbilt will define the great university of the 21st Century and be it. Managers who turn AI signals into real staffing moves are how Exceptional Core Operations keeps its footing while the work itself changes. This month serves Goal 3, AI-Enabled Workforce Readiness.
facilitate: Read the mission line slowly, once; name the goal, once.
No discussion here; the whole slide is under a minute.
sections.transition: Here is what you will be able to do in 45 minutes.

sections.title: Objectives
sections.purpose: Set the contract for the session in about a minute; this slide is also the roadmap.
sections.say: By the end of this session you will be able to: name the four workforce moves: reskill, redeploy, redesign, and hire; match one ai-exposure insight from your team to the move it calls for; commit to one move with a named owner and a real date. We take them in order, and each one has something to practice.
facilitate: Read the three objectives briskly; they double as the agenda.
Point at the goal chip once, then move.

sections.title: The four moves
sections.purpose: Install the shared vocabulary: reskill, redeploy, redesign, hire, and the order to try them in.
sections.say: In April you built an exposure map: which work on your team AI touches most. Maps are not moves. This month gives the map a verb, and there are only four worth learning: reskill the person, redeploy the strength, redesign the role, hire what you cannot build. The order matters as much as the list. When McKinsey surveyed companies closing skill gaps, reskilling the people they already had usually beat hiring on both cost and fit, which is why hire sits last today.
facilitate: Walk the four moves once, one line each; resist the urge to lecture.
Read the In the room card aloud; everyone holds one real role in mind and names their instinct move silently.
Lead the discussion prompt, two or three voices, then run the breakout: which move most, which never?

ask.q: Which of the four moves does your team reach for first, honestly?
expect: Hire, because it feels like the real solution
Reskill, because training requests are easy to make
ask.respond: Most rooms admit to hire-first. The order flips that default: the cheapest moves use the people already on your team.

sections.debrief: Four verbs, tried in order of what you already have. That order is the discipline of this month.
sections.watchFor: Managers treating the moves as HR paperwork categories. Keep them as verbs a manager can start this week.
sections.transition: Vocabulary done. Now the skill: matching a real insight to its move.
sections.coreNote: Core: skip the breakout; take two discussion answers in chat.

sections.title: The match
sections.purpose: Practice matching an AI-exposure insight to the move it calls for.
sections.say: Here is the skill this month actually asks of you: read what a signal says about the work, then call the move. We will do three together. Notice that hire is off the board for all three; that is deliberate. Hire is real, and it comes after the other three have been honestly tried.
facilitate: Run Call the move live; everyone plays on their own screen.
After round two, pause: ask who called it differently and why. The disagreement is the teaching.
Run the breakout: one real insight, role only, partner challenges the call.

ask.q: Why is redeploy the least used move in most departments?
expect: We think in roles, so freed capacity looks like slack
Managers fear losing the person to another team
ask.respond: Both true. Redeploy asks you to see strengths as portable. The Transfer Portal thinking from the fall applies inside your own team too.

sections.debrief: Reskill grows the person with the work. Redeploy points a strength at new work. Redesign rebuilds the role. Say the reason out loud when you call the move; the reason is the match.
sections.watchFor: Anyone naming a struggling teammate by name in the breakout. Redirect warmly: roles, never names.
sections.transition: You can call the move. Now it needs an owner and a date, or it stays a slide.
sections.coreNote: Core: run the trainer, skip the breakout, one voice on the debrief.

sections.title: Owner and date
sections.purpose: Convert one matched move into a sentence with an owner and a date.
sections.say: The distance between an insight and an action is one sentence: the move, a role, a reason, then an owner and a date. Vague versions of that sentence survive meetings for years. We are going to build the sharp version and put step one on a real calendar.
facilitate: Run Write the move; give the room two minutes to make both choices and run it.
Ask one volunteer to read a strong outcome aloud.
Point at the pattern: specific sentence, named owner, dated step one.

ask.q: Why does 'the team needs to reskill around AI' fail as a move?
expect: No person, no skill, no date
Nobody can tell later whether it happened
ask.respond: Right. A move you cannot verify later was never a move. Specific enough to check is the bar.

sections.debrief: One sentence, one owner, one date. If it will not fit that shape, it is still an insight.
sections.watchFor: Owners who are always the manager. Push at least step two toward the person whose work is changing; it is their move too.
sections.transition: Quick recap, then you build your own move card.
sections.coreNote: Core: everyone runs the builder solo; skip the read-aloud.

sections.title: The core idea
sections.purpose: Land the one sentence the session exists to install.
sections.say: If you keep one sentence from today, this is it. Read it once, out loud: Match each AI insight to one of the four moves, then give it an owner and a date.
facilitate: Pause two beats after reading; the word animation carries it.
sections.coreNote: Core: pass through in stride; the sentence reads itself.

sections.title: Recap quiz
sections.purpose: Score the learning while it is fresh; wrong answers are teaching moments, not failures.
sections.say: Three questions, on your own screen. Answer honestly; the explanations are where the learning sticks.
facilitate: Give the room 90 seconds to run it individually.
Ask for a show of results in chat: how many got 3 of 3?
Read out the explanation for whichever question drew the most misses.
sections.watchFor: Rushing past the why lines. The explanations carry the teaching.
sections.transition: Now point it at your real week.

sections.title: Capstone commitment
sections.purpose: Convert the session into one named, dated action per person.
sections.say: Now the real one. Take the sharpest insight from your April exposure map, role only. Call its move, name the owner, pick the window, build the card, and copy it somewhere you will see it before Friday. Two minutes, quiet, go.
facilitate: Two quiet minutes; everyone builds their own card.
Invite two or three volunteers to read their card aloud or paste it in chat.
Remind: copy the card somewhere you will see it this week.
sections.watchFor: Vague entries. Nudge for a name-able situation and a real date.

sections.title: Closing
sections.purpose: End with the next step and where this thread continues.
sections.say: This series year opened with seeing talent. It wraps this month with moving on what you see. Hold step one this week. Tomorrow's Take-Off Tuesday has everyone, your team included, building a personal 90-day AI action plan; point your people at it. Thursday's Thrive Thursday wraps the series year with decisiveness, moving from data to move, which is this exact muscle. And for a longer runway, this month's LinkedIn Learning course, Leading Your Team Through Change, and the navigator-led action-planning lab are built for the move you just wrote.
facilitate: Point at the next-step card; one sentence.
Name the rest of the week's rhythm: the other sessions echo this month's theme.
